questiontext.text: In the Latin-square decomposition, a magic square is built from...

feedback.text: Correct — a Graeco-Latin (Euler) square is a pair of orthogonal Latin squares.
One permutation cannot guarantee the magic property.
Factorization is unrelated to this construction.

answer.text: a sorted list of the values

feedback.text: Sorting does not produce a magic square.

generalfeedback.text: Two orthogonal Latin squares combine into a Graeco-Latin square, from which the magic square is read off.

questiontext.text: If a and b are the symbols from the two Latin squares at a cell, the magic-square value there is...

feedback.text: Correct — the pair (a, b) becomes a base-n digit combination.
Simple addition loses the one-to-one mapping of pairs.
Multiplying the symbols does not give distinct values.
Subtraction does not yield the 0..n^2-1 range.

generalfeedback.text: Reading (a, b) as a two-digit base-n number, value = a*n + b, gives every value once when the squares are orthogonal.

questiontext.text: What defines a Latin square of order n?

answer.text: each symbol appears exactly once in every row and every column

feedback.text: Correct — that is the Latin-square condition.

answer.text: each symbol appears once in the whole grid

feedback.text: Symbols repeat across the grid; the rule is per row and per column.

answer.text: the diagonals contain only one symbol

feedback.text: Latin squares constrain rows and columns, not a single diagonal symbol.
Identical rows would repeat symbols in columns.

generalfeedback.text: A Latin square has each of its n symbols exactly once per row and once per column.

answer.text: every ordered pair (a, b) of symbols occurs exactly once

feedback.text: Correct — that is the definition of orthogonal Latin squares.
Identical squares are not orthogonal.
Reversal does not ensure all pairs appear once.

answer.text: they share no common symbol set

feedback.text: They use the same symbol set; orthogonality is about pairings.

generalfeedback.text: Superimposing orthogonal squares yields each of the n^2 ordered pairs exactly once — a Graeco-Latin square.

questiontext.text: In a Latin square, each symbol appears exactly once in every row and once in every column.

feedback.text: Correct — that is the defining property.
This is precisely the Latin-square rule.

questiontext.text: The Latin-square decomposition needs only one Latin square to form the magic square.

feedback.text: It needs two orthogonal Latin squares combined via a*n + b.
Correct — a pair of orthogonal Latin squares is required.

questiontext.text: A grid in which each symbol occurs exactly once per row and once per column is called a ______ square.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the Latin-square decomposition are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: The value at a cell is a*n + b from the two squares

feedback.text: Yes — a base-n combination of the pair.

answer.text: Each symbol appears once per row and once per column

feedback.text: Yes — the Latin-square condition.

answer.text: Only one Latin square is required

feedback.text: No — two orthogonal Latin squares are needed.

answer.text: The value at a cell is the product a*b

feedback.text: No — it is a*n + b, not a*b.

generalfeedback.text: Two orthogonal Latin squares combine as a*n + b; each symbol appears once per row and column.
